outcome.candidate_text:
For each fixed \(x\in[0,1)\), we have \(x^n\to 0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Suppose the convergence were uniform. Take \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every positive integer \(N\), let \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}\). Then \(x\in[0,1)\), so \(f(x)=0\), but
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\frac12.
\]
Hence no \(N\) can ensure \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\tfrac12\) for all \(n\ge N\) and all \(x\in[0,1]\). Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).
outcome.stop_reason: The proof first identifies the unique possible limit and then directly negates the definition of uniform convergence using a fixed positive tolerance.
